source_refs.note: Book p. 259-260: unit introduction; 14.1 scalars and vectors, 2D addition, scalar multiple, equal and parallel vectors, magnitude in 2D, 3 figures. Book error: 'parallel to AB - BA'. Teaching notes, Key points, Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: Introduction

In this unit, we look into the rectangular coordinate system in three-dimensional space and explore the fundamental mathematical operations involving vectors in space. We begin by understanding the dot product (or scalar product) and the cross product (or vector product) of two vectors and learn about their geometric interpretation. Further, we emphasize their practical applications: for example, how these concepts are used to calculate the area of a triangle and the area of a parallelogram. Finally, we explore the extensive use of vectors in three-dimensional space, particularly in physics, where they play an important role in determining forces, velocities and other essential physical quantities, for example the work done by a constant force when moving an object along a specified vector.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How this unit is built: 14.1 recalls vectors from earlier classes and carries them into space (three coordinates instead of two); 14.2 is the dot product; 14.3 is the cross product; 14.4 is the scalar triple product.
Notation: the book writes a vector with a line under its letter, \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{i}\). Other books use bold letters or an arrow, \(\vec{u}\); they all mean the same thing. \(\underline{AB}\) is the vector that starts at \(A\) and ends at \(B\). In your notebook always mark a vector (underline or arrow); a letter without the mark is just a number.

In previous classes, we learned about two fundamental quantities: scalars and vectors. A scalar is a quantity that has only magnitude or size, such as mass, time, density, temperature, length, volume, speed, work etc. On the other hand, a vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, for example displacement, velocity, acceleration, weight, force, momentum, electric and magnetic fields, etc.
Geometrically, a vector is represented as a directed line segment \(\underline{AB}\) with \(A\) as its initial point and \(B\) as the terminal point.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why an arrow? The length of the arrow shows the magnitude and the arrowhead shows the direction. So \(\underline{AB}\) and \(\underline{BA}\) have the same length but opposite directions: \(\underline{BA} = -\underline{AB}\).
A quick test for scalar or vector: ask \"in which direction?\". \"5 kg in which direction?\" makes no sense, so mass is a scalar. \"20 N in which direction?\" matters (a push up or down is different), so force is a vector.

In two dimensions (\(R^{2}\)) a vector has components that can be represented by an ordered pair \([x, y]\) of real numbers. For the vector \(\underline{u} = [x, y]\), \(x\) and \(y\) represent the components of \(\underline{u}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Both rules work component by component: first components together, second components together.
\([2, 3] + [4, -1] = [2 + 4,\ 3 + (-1)] = [6, 2]\)
\(3[2, -1] = [3 \times 2,\ 3 \times (-1)] = [6, -3]\)
Picture: adding is walking along \(\underline{u}\) and then along \(\underline{v}\); multiplying by 3 stretches the arrow to three times its length (a negative number also turns it round).

Equal Vectors: Two vectors \(\underline{u} = [x_{1}, y_{1}]\) and \(\underline{v} = [x_{2}, y_{2}]\) of \(R^{2}\) are said to be equal if and only if they have the same components. That is, \([x_{1}, y_{1}] = [x_{2}, y_{2}]\) if and only if \(x_{1} = x_{2}\) and \(y_{1} = y_{2}\), and we write \(\underline{u} = \underline{v}\).
In other words, two vectors \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) are said to be equal if they have the same magnitude and the same direction.

blocks.alt: Two arrows of the same length pointing in the same direction (up and to the left): AB from A to B and CD from C to D, drawn side by side.
blocks.caption: Equal vectors AB and CD: same length and same direction, different positions (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In the figure \(\underline{AB}\) and \(\underline{CD}\) start at different points, yet they are equal: only length and direction matter, not where the arrow is drawn. You may slide a vector anywhere without turning or stretching it.

Parallel Vectors: Two vectors are parallel if and only if they are non-zero scalar multiples of each other.
For example, vectors \(-\underline{AB}\) and \(\frac{3}{2}\underline{AB}\) are parallel to \(\underline{AB} - \underline{BA}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book ends the sentence with \"parallel to \(\underline{AB} - \underline{BA}\)\". The figure shows \(\underline{AB}\), \(-\underline{AB}\) and \(\frac{3}{2}\underline{AB}\), so the intended statement is: \(-\underline{AB}\) and \(\frac{3}{2}\underline{AB}\) are parallel to \(\underline{AB}\). (Since \(\underline{BA} = -\underline{AB}\), the printed \(\underline{AB} - \underline{BA}\) equals \(2\underline{AB}\), which is also parallel, but that is not what the sentence means.)

blocks.alt: Three arrows on parallel slanting lines: AB pointing up to the right, minus AB of the same length pointing down to the left, and three halves AB pointing up to the right and one and a half times as long.
blocks.caption: Parallel vectors AB, −AB and (3/2)AB (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to test two vectors for being parallel: divide component by component. If all the ratios are equal, the vectors are parallel.
\([-3, 6]\) and \([2, -4]\): \(\frac{-3}{2} = \frac{6}{-4} = -\frac{3}{2}\), so \([-3, 6] = -\frac{3}{2}[2, -4]\): parallel.
A positive multiple points the same way; a negative multiple points the opposite way (like \(-\underline{AB}\) in the figure).
Magnitude of a Vector

The magnitude (or norm or length) of a vector in 2D represents the length of the vector from the origin to the point represented by the vector. For any vector \(\underline{u} = [x, y]\) in \(R^{2}\), we define the magnitude as the distance of the point \(P(x, y)\) from the origin \(O\).

blocks.text_alt: magnitude of OP equals magnitude of u equals the square root of x squared plus y squared

blocks.alt: x and y axes with origin O. A blue arrow goes from O to the point P(x, y). A vertical blue segment of length y drops from P to the x-axis, making a right angle; the horizontal leg along the x-axis has length x. The arrow is labelled square root of x squared plus y squared.
blocks.caption: Magnitude of u = [x, y]: the length OP of the hypotenuse, √(x² + y²) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where does \(\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\) come from? In the figure, the legs of the right triangle are \(x\) and \(y\), and \(OP\) is the hypotenuse. Pythagoras gives \(OP^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}\).
Examples: \(|[3, 4]| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5\); \(|[-5, 12]| = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13\). A negative component gives the same square, because a length is never negative.
Now, we will learn some mathematical operations involving vectors in three-dimensional space.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.
\(\underline{AB}\) starts at \(A\) and ends at \(B\); \(\underline{BA} = -\underline{AB}\).
Add vectors and multiply by scalars component by component.
Equal vectors: same components, that is, same length and same direction.
Parallel vectors: one is a non-zero scalar multiple of the other.
\(|[x, y]| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Adding magnitudes instead of vectors: \(|\underline{u} + \underline{v}|\) is generally not \(|\underline{u}| + |\underline{v}|\). For \([3, 0] + [0, 4] = [3, 4]\) the magnitude is 5, not \(3 + 4 = 7\).
Forgetting to square a negative component: \(|[-5, 12]|\) uses \((-5)^{2} = 25\), not \(-25\).
Thinking \(\underline{AB}\) and \(\underline{BA}\) are equal: they point opposite ways.
